sg.title: Today's big idea
sg.text: Good readers find what the text says AND what it suggests, then prove it with evidence.

sg.title: Notes
sg.text:
An inference is a smart guess based on [[evidence|clues]] and what you already know.
You prove it by [[citing|quoting]] the text.

sg.title: Watch me
sg.text:
The story says: "Her lungs burned before she reached the corner."
Step 1: What does the text say? Her lungs burned quickly.
Step 2: What do I know? Burning lungs mean you're out of breath.
Step 3: Inference: **Maya is not used to running yet.**

sg.title: Try it with me
sg.text: "He stared at it, his stomach twisting." Theo feels [[worried|guilty|nervous|upset]].

sg.title: Stop and jot
sg.text: What is the difference between what a text says and what it suggests?

days.race: What does Coach Rivera mean when she says, "Last isn't the same as done"? Use evidence from the story.

passage.title: The Last Lap
passage.text:
Maya had never run a full mile without stopping. Every afternoon, she watched the cross-country team loop around the track while she sat on the bleachers with her sketchbook.

"You could try out," Coach Rivera said one day, pausing beside her. Maya laughed and shook her head. "I'm not a runner," she said.

But that night, she laced up her old sneakers and jogged to the end of her street. Her lungs burned before she reached the corner. She walked home slowly, embarrassed, but the next night she went a little farther.

For three weeks, Maya added one mailbox at a time. Some nights it rained, and some nights her legs felt like concrete. She kept going anyway.

On tryout day, Maya finished last. Her face was red and her shirt was soaked, but she had run the entire mile. Coach Rivera wrote something on her clipboard and smiled. "Last isn't the same as done," she said. "See you Monday."

sg.title: Today's big idea
sg.text: Strong claims are backed by reasons and evidence. Weak claims are not.

sg.title: Notes
sg.text:
A supported claim has [[evidence|facts|a source]].
"Everyone knows" usually signals an [[unsupported|opinion]] claim.

sg.title: Watch me
sg.text:
Is "Some schools reported better attendance" supported?
Step 1: Is there a fact or source? Yes, schools reported it.
Step 2: Could we check it? Yes.
Step 3: **Supported.**

sg.title: Try it with me
sg.text: "Starting later is simply the right thing to do." This claim is [[unsupported|not supported]].

days.race: Is the author's argument convincing? Evaluate one claim that is supported by evidence and one that is not.

passage.title: Later Start Times Would Help Students
passage.text:
Many middle schools start before eight in the morning. I believe schools should start later so students can get the sleep they need.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start at 8:30 or later. Doctors say that preteens need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night, but many get far less.

When students are tired, they have a harder time paying attention and remembering what they learn. Some schools that moved their start times later reported better attendance.

Some people argue that later start times would make after-school sports end too late. However, schools could adjust practice schedules, and a rested athlete is a better athlete.

Besides, everyone knows that students are happier in the morning when they can sleep in. Starting later is simply the right thing to do.

days.race: How does the waggle dance help a hive survive? Use evidence from the text.

passage.title: Why Honeybees Dance
passage.text:
A honeybee that finds a good patch of flowers has a problem: how can it tell the rest of the hive where to go? Bees cannot draw maps or speak. Instead, they dance.

Scientists call it the waggle dance. The bee walks in a straight line while shaking its body, then circles back and repeats the move. The direction of the straight line shows the direction of the flowers compared to the sun.

The length of the waggle tells the distance. A longer waggle means the flowers are farther away. Other bees crowd around the dancer, feel its movements in the dark hive, and then fly off to find the food.

Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, spent years studying this behavior. In 1973, he shared the Nobel Prize for his work. Before his research, many people did not believe insects could share such detailed information.

Today, scientists still study the waggle dance. Understanding how bees find food may help farmers protect these insects, which pollinate many of the crops people eat.
